utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And just to mention that Judge Orie is not with us this morning for urgent personal business, and Judge Fluegge and I have decided that in the interests of justice we sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis so that we do not waste time. We have heard of no preliminaries from either side. May the witness please be called in. But before we do that, can we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, you have testified here before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Under protective measures of pseudonym and face distortion. Those protective measures will continue to be applied in this hearing. Because of the pseudonym protective measures, you will be referred to as GRM097. Your name will not be mentioned. Please help the Chamber by also making sure that you do not say anything during your testimony that may reveal your identity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You will now be examined first by Mr. Ivetic. I see he is standing. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the team of Mr. Mladic's Defence. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to first ask for 1D4146 in e-court, but it should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I would ask you to look at the sheet that is on the screen in front of you. And if you can confirm for us if your personal details are accurately recorded therein.

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: They are accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document under seal as the next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ivetic. Madam Registrar, may you please give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D04146 receives Exhibit Number D1297.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exhibit D1297 is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to take a look at 1D4147 on the screen. And if it's easier, I also have a hard copy, with the assistance of the usher, which we can provide to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I take it this is not being broadcast either.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's -- agreed, should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, now on the screen and in hard copy, I would ask you do you recognise this written statement which you have before you?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: I do recognise it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 4 in e-court, which is the last page in the hard copy. And again, none of this should be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm for us whose signature appears on this last page of the statement?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Since signing this statement on the date that is entered on this last page, have you had a chance to look through your entire statement to see if everything is correctly written therein?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Yes, at the time I signed it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you stand by everything as being correct as of the date of the giving of this statement?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I were to ask you questions today arising out of the same factual scenarios as in your written statement, would your answers today to those questions be the same in substance as contained in your written statement?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: They would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Insofar as you have taken a declaration to tell the truth today, does that mean that what is written in your statement is also truthful in nature?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender under seal the document before us, 1D4147, as the next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, may you please give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives Exhibit Number D1298, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And D1298 is admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And Your Honours we would tender also under seal 1D4148 which is the document that is referenced in the footnotes of the statement which we've just admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any objection, Madam? It's admitted. May it please be given a number, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. At this time, I have a short summary of the statement without any identifying information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: GRM097 was deployed to the former Yugoslavia as an UNPROFOR member in 1994 among other deployments. He notes the Serbs were already being blamed for the Markale shelling on 6 February 1994. Although the assumption was that the Serbs were responsible, UNPROFOR began receiving information that cast doubt on that assumption. It was highly unusual that the Serbs would fire a single round. Given that the height and proximity of buildings to the place where the shell landed, the shell would have come at a very high trajectory, suggesting that it had been fired at close range. UNPROFOR also received information that the shell may have been fired by a Mujahedin group who missed their target. At several meetings with the Bosnian government, General Rose even told the Bosnians that evidence was emerging that the market-place shelling may have been carried out by their side. All the circumstances led the witness to believe that in all probability it was not the Serbs who fired the shell on Markale market. Further, the Bosnian government pursued a strategy of trying to blame Serbs for atrocities in order to obtain international intervention on their side. And that completes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask some follow-up questions. If we could first --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just before we go a little bit further and so it doesn't get sort of swept away, could we deal for a moment with the associated exhibits that my friend tendered. D0414 -- pardon me, 1D04148 has just been admitted, but what's been uploaded in e-court doesn't appear to be what 1D04148 has been represented to be. 1D04148, as it's been uploaded, is a photograph. If we could just have a check of that and perhaps deal with it as we go on, but I just wanted to raise the matter before we dealt with the evidence in more detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It should not be the photograph. It should be another document. I suggest that we then -- I suggest that we vacate, for the time being, that document that's been given that number, and then at the break I will check to see what the correct information is and we'll -- or just wait. We could just wait. I'll deal with it at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's wait and you can deal with it after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- and again, we should not broadcast the statement, but I'd like to call up the statement which is now D1298 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to talk about paragraph number 6 of that statement. And here you say, and I quote: "Although the assumption was that the Serbs were responsible for this shelling, we began to receive information which cast doubt upon that assumption. This information was relayed to us via various reports which were briefed to the General during his routine daily staff updates and his intelligence staff." Can you tell us anything about how reliable the sources of these reports were considered to be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But we've just -- if we could go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us anything about how reliable the sources of these reports were considered to be within UNPROFOR; that is to say, the reports casting doubt on the responsibility of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: There was a significant amount of information being circulated at the time. The reliability of the sources, you know, at times is questionable, that's why all the information would have been checked. You mentioned the -- one of the options that we understood was -- what happened was that the Mujahedin group, which we'd not seen in Sarajevo, had targeted a -- a group of Jews leaving the city. That was just one report that came in which we then couldn't verify. Other reports then came from in from Sector Sarajevo from the French headquarters, from the UNMOs who were stationed around -- around the city. We also had our own national intelligence sources that we were fed into the headquarters. And again, they were at the same time looking at the totality of information based on different sources and making judgements. So, it was, you know, throughout the whole period we, on the day of the market massacre, weren't actually in the city. We were in Croatia and then moved into Bosnia to be with the Bosnian Croats in and around Mostar. And so it was only then when we got back to the headquarters the following day, on the 6th, that the General was then appraised of the totality of the situation, the investigations that had taken place. And throughout the whole course of that day and the days following, the weight of the evidence was suggesting that it wasn't carried out by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now in paragraph number 7, starting on the last two lines -- two words on this page and bleeding on to the next page, it is said: "The initial assessment (redacted) was that if it was a mortar round that had been fired by the Serbs, the firing point would have been at the most forward of their front line. Mortars are doctrinally deployed in depth, to the rear of the forward trenches, but within their effective ranges for their own force protection." Can you explain for us why per doctrine mortars are deployed in depth?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: Very simply, in terms of you would make maximum uses of the ranges available to you. Somewhere like Sarajevo, for example, different parts of the city could be targeted by different firing positions. What you wouldn't want to do was to have your fire-power deployed forward, which would make it vulnerable first of all to counter-battery fire if it was within range of your own mortar position, but also, more importantly, vulnerable to potential infiltration or infantry assault. So given that any artillery or mortar position would have to be properly bedded in, properly safeguarded in terms of protection, and therefore the last thing that you wanted to do, necessarily, was to keep moving it. Although, with mortars, that's the benefit of that fire system. It could be easily quickly deployed. So you would have it in depth, ideally in dead ground. Certainly not in a forward position that would make it vulnerable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please, for a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in this paragraph you describe the buildings and their proximity to where the shell landed at the market. Did you have occasion to visit the site or is this information based upon what others had told you?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: We had occasion to visit the site. It was in the centre of the city, and so shortly thereafter, I think literally on the next day when

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: think, visited the site. And obviously, you know, throughout the whole war while I was there for that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now you've already mentioned one of the ultimate reports talking about it being an errant shell being from a Mujahedin group that had missed their target. What information did UNPROFOR have as to the Mujahedin in Bosnia or in to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: With regards to the whole presence of Mujahedin around Bosnia, I'm not entirely sure of the exact details. All I can do is reference you to my own experiences. Prior to this operational tour, I was operating in Central Bosnia, and we did come across them in Central Bosnia, both, you know, home-grown Mujahedin in many respects and also foreign fighters. But we -- certainly during the period of time that we were in Sarajevo, I didn't see any in Sarajevo. So this was a report that came in from one of our sources, and then after that it was probably discounted on the grounds that it couldn't be verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you identified the totality of the reporting and the circumstances earlier. Did the totality of the reporting arriving at UNPROFOR discuss, apart from this potential Mujahedin source, did it discuss any other alternate sources for the shell in question?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: As I said, there was different viewpoints. Some said it was detonated in situ. Some said it was obviously fired from, you know, within the city itself to make it look as if it was the Serbs. There was also reports that it was -- the mortar was thrown or a device was thrown from the building immediately to its front, to the north -- north-east, wherever it was. But again, some of these couldn't be verified. There was an analysis carried out by an artillery officer from within the headquarters who -- his assessment at the time was that, based on his experience and his understanding, that it was then fired from the Serb side as opposed to any of the two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph number 10, which is on this page, and I won't mention the name of the individual, but in relation to saying that the Serbs were guilty of the previous shelling and that there was an inference to this incident. First of all, to what previous shelling does your statement refer to?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: The -- the day before the attack on the Markale market-place, there was a shelling of Dobrinja, which is one of suburbs of Sarajevo, close to the airport, where on that occasion around five mortar rounds landed killing about ten people and wounded a number more. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we may want to do a redaction to be on the safe side as to line 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And you will remember the two redactions, Madam Registrar. Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dealing just briefly with the Dobrinja shelling we've just discussed, was there an analysis performed of that shelling by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: There was by Sector Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall who would have performed that analysis?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: Colonel Sonnic, who was the Chief of Staff of Sector Sarajevo, was present at the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there any armija BiH units or facilities in the Dobrinja neighbourhood that UNPROFOR had knowledge of?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: Yes, there was. There was at least a brigade formation, an infantry brigade, in Dobrinja, which we visited after the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you have any knowledge of where those units were situated in Dobrinja in relation to where the shelling occurred?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: Not exactly, but they were in and around the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, returning to Markale. Based on the totality of the reporting that was coming into UNPROFOR about this incident, what was the vibe or feeling of others in UNPROFOR as to who was ultimately responsible for that shelling?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: As I said, within the headquarters, as the information kept coming in, it was being verified, was being examined by the G2, the intelligence staff within the headquarters, and the briefings took place which suggested that it had been carried out by the -- by the Bosnians themselves, Bosnian Muslims themselves. It was quite an extraordinary sort of feeling at that time that we'd heard previously on arrival when we were briefed that the Bosnian government side were prone to staging events, you know, and this, of course, was our first real example where, you know, they'd potentially fired upon their own people, whether it was directed or whether it was carried out by another agency of the Bosnian government without, dare I say, the official sanction of the president or whoever. But it was, you know, quite unbelievable sort of atmosphere in the headquarters when we were realising the extent of, A, the tragedy, and who perpetrated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now taking into account the time of your entire deployment to the theatre, did you have any other instances or facts that you experienced that led you to conclude that the BiH side was engaging in shelling its own territory in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: That's obviously a difficult question to answer. But certainly, you know, whenever something was going to be taking place, you know, it's always convenient that Sarajevo would be shelled. This is one of the reasons why mortar-locating radar was brought into the city very shortly after the cease-fire to start verifying where rounds were coming from. And from the reports that those radar operators gleaned from their systems, on a number of occasions they did discover that mortar rounds were fired from within the city at certain targets. I always remember, I can't recall when it was, seeing a -- a news report on television where the back of the Presidency building was being filmed, static filming. There was no interviews taking place but just a camera pointing at the Presidency building, and the rocket then suddenly hits literally the centre of the frame. Which again, you know, a rocket coming at low altitude could only have come from a certain area of the city so close to the Presidency building. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we can go into private session for some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 15 of your statement you talk about experiences in Sarajevo that the Bosnian government pursued a strategy of trying to blame Serbs for atrocities in order to obtain international intervention. You say examples of this were the ongoing fire of mortars from schools, hospitals, and other civilian areas and from areas adjacent to UN positions, which would draw return fire from the Serbs in those areas. And you also say that: "Throughout the subsequent cease-fire for Sarajevo, signed by both sides, the Bosnian Government Military were guilty of the vast majority of the breaches of its terms." Now, in relation to the cease-fire that was signed and that is the subject matter of this paragraph, what was UNPROFOR's stated position as to what would happen if a side failed to adhere to the terms of that agreement?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: The agreement was equally applicable to the Bosnian government as it was to the Bosnian Serbs, and the NATO ultimatum certainly in terms of the withdrawal of heavy weapons and the compliance to the terms of the agreement was reaffirmed. And certainly one of the press briefings that General Rose gave with Vice-President Ganic, where Vice-President Ganic said that General Rose would carry out the agreement to the word should the Serbs not comply. And General Rose, in front of the press, again confirmed that it was equally applicable to the Bosnian government side as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the outgoing fire that you identify in this paragraph from civilian areas, was the intensity of the same affected by any events in particular?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: I think you have to realise that the Bosnian government was physically located in amongst its own people, because that's how they were. At the end of the day, the Serbs were outside the city or within suburbs of the city itself. And therefore, when I refer to firing amongst the, you know, the civilian population, that's because that's how they were physically deployed. There wasn't a delineation of civilians and military. They were -- they were mixed together. And so, you know, around this time immediately prior to the, you know -- from the point when we first arrived, very soon thereafter there were certainly sniper fire and outgoing sort of mortar rounds from behind our building, in our view, designed to create a retaliation from the Bosnian Serb side. And then during the actual cease-fire itself, as it was put into place, there was a number of violations which we constantly complained to the Bosnian government on, the fact that the Bosnians were breaking this -- breaching this cease-fire with a view to provoking the Serbs into retaliation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now during your deployment as part of UNPROFOR, were NATO air strikes against the Bosnian Muslim side ever ordered or requested by UNPROFOR for breaches of the cease-fire agreement that you've just discussed?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: Not in relation to the cease-fire. Prior to the use of close air support in Gorazde, that was the first time that NATO had -- in support of the United Nations had used close air support. But as early on as February, maybe early March, there were two occasions where UN forces were being attacked by, in one case the Bosnian Croats, first of all, in the area of Fojnica, and then what we believed were Bosnian government forces in the region of Ribnica. Close air support was requested for those acts but wasn't carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge -- or what was your knowledge of the position of NATO as to the prospect of carrying out air strikes against the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: I had, you know -- I had no talks with NATO commanders. That was something which was done at the higher levels. But all of us realised that it was highly unlikely that NATO would strike Bosnian government forces irrespective of the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 16 of your statement, which we also should not broadcast, you talk about the Bosnian government refusing to approve a water system established by an American humanitarian activist in the pretext that the water was not clean enough. And you say "because the government did not want to alleviate the suffering of civilians in Sarajevo." Can you explain for us what you mean here when you say "the government did not want to alleviate the suffering of civilians in Sarajevo"?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: The impact of the cease-fire, from our perspective, was an opportunity to return the city to normality. And one of the things which the people were desperate for, given the time of year, was for their electricity to be able to be turned on, particularly at night, for the gas to come on, and for them to have running water. Because at this stage, obviously for the last 18 months or however long it was, people were having to go down to the river, which was unclean, in order to get their water. And so one of the things which we had an issue with with the Bosnian government was the fact that the US government through Fred Cuny, who was a US government employee, had established this water treatment plant designed to purify the water, which could have -- when turned on would be able to give a substantial part of the population clean running water and therefore wouldn't need them to go to the river to get the actual water supplies. And literally, you know, in fact Madeleine Albright, when she visited Sarajevo with General Shalikashvili, went to visit this water treatment plant because it was, you know, such an important facility. And then as soon as it was finished, they turned the water on, and the Bosnian government refused to allow them to supply its own people with water. They said it wasn't clean enough, which was ridiculous. And certainly our view was because we'd effectively established a cease-fire, therefore Sarajevo now wasn't in the news for the reasons that the Bosnian government wanted Sarajevo, let's say, to be in the news, to maintain a narrative of a city under siege, you know, people suffering. People were now walking the streets, and so this eroded the narrative from the government perspective. And this was yet another example where they wanted the suffering to continue because that's what hit the headlines, and of course it was something which, from a UN perspective, we were all trying to end. We were -- we wanted to restore normality as best we could for the people themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Witness, it's time to take a break. We'll come back in 20 minutes' time. But before you leave the room, could we please go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Mr. Ivetic, I'm sure you want to continue --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you had previously mentioned mortar-identifying radar in Sarajevo. Who was it that operated that mortar-firing identification radar?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: They were members of the British army contingent of UNPROFOR from the Royal Regiment of Royal Artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were there any instances that you recall where the reporting of outgoing rounds from Sarajevo by UNMO differed from that which was being otherwise reported or known to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: We were only there for a relatively short period of time when there was fire taking place in Sarajevo because of the -- the cease-fire. But immediately the night before the -- on -- I think it was the first day after the cease-fire had taken place, that evening we heard from behind, again, the residency, the fact that mortar rounds had been fired towards the Bosnian Serb positions. Complaints were made to the Bosnian government Ministry of Defence through their liaison officer, Chef de Cabinet Zijad Sisic, that these fire breaches were taking place. General Divjak still at that time had responsibility for negotiations with us. He complained that we were not reporting cease-fire violations by the Bosnian Serb army. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you go on, I'm not sure you answered the question and I'm also not sure what the question was. Mr. Ivetic, you question was: "Were there any instances that you recall where the reporting of outgoing rounds from Sarajevo by UNMO ..." Were there shots -- rounds fired by UNMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The reporting by UNMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around -- around the city of Sarajevo, we had the United Nations Monitoring Officers deployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But then the question continues to say whether they differed from that which was being otherwise reported or known to UNPROFOR. I'm not sure whether that answer -- this answers that part of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe the witness has stated that the reporting was of 11 incoming rounds as opposed to outgoing rounds, when in fact the knowledge was that they were outgoing rounds, based upon the activities that the witness described and the complaints made to the Bosnian government Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I thought your question was intended to find out -- to get a comparison between the firing which was being reported otherwise or known to UNPROFOR in comparison with what the reporting they had received. But if you're satisfied with the answer, I'm happy with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I need one clarification further from the witness. When he says it was reported that there were 11 incoming rounds as opposed to outgoing rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Who was reporting the 11 incoming rounds as opposed to outgoing rounds?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And let's go briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, first of all we're in open session, so please be careful of what you say so as not to personally identify yourself. In relation to the close air support around Gorazde in 1994, how did the Bosnian Serb army perceive UNPROFOR after commencement of that air support?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: The view was that we'd sided with the Bosnian government against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what actions were taken by the Serb side with respect to UN personnel?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: We had at that stage roughly 150 military observers or soldiers from UNPROFOR who were either acting as observers or safeguarding the weapon collection points in terms of maintaining control, and they were all effectively detained, effectively, in a hostage-type situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how were they treated when they were so detained?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: As far as we were concerned they were well treated. I don't think that the soldiers themselves or the Bosnian Serb military viewed them as combatants in that physical role. I think their issue was more with the United Nations hierarchy, which was ourselves, who had ordered the close air support on their forces around Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in terms of communications emanating from the Serb side, how did they refer to the situation and react?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: We -- we were openly described by General Mladic as aggressors who had, you know, who had struck the Serbian people, and therefore he demanded that we stop all air action against his forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to Sarajevo, and you earlier talked about weapon collection points, I'd like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: D112 in e-court. I also have a hard copy, with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is -- while we wait for you to get the hard copy, this is dated 16 August 1994, from Akashi to Annan, and it discusses weapon collection points and the problem caused by BiH threats and potential BiH violations of the exclusion zone. And here on the first page, it says essentially prompting the BSA to seek to withdraw weapons from weapon collection points. On the second page of this document, if we can go to that, it says in the paragraph number 3 that -- it talks about an attachment protocol which recognises the BSA's legitimate right of self-defence if they come under pressure from the BiH. First of all, sir, prior to yesterday in proofing with myself, had you ever seen this cable, the first two pages of which we have now seen in e-court and the hard copy of which is in your hands?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: I have not -- I wasn't in Bosnia in August, so I've not seen the first two pages. I've seen the third page which were the points of the agreement. I hadn't previously seen the protocol, which is dated 19th of February, because I wasn't at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, have you had a chance to read through the protocol of understanding which is, I believe, page 4 in e-court and 5 in e-court of this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what are your comments of how this protocol either compares or departs from the actual situation on the ground relating to enforcement of the weapon collection points?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: The protocol is in line with the principle of the establishment of the weapon collection points. You will recall originally the Bosnian government request was to have all their weapons -- all the Bosnian Serb weapons withdrawn 30 kilometres from Sarajevo. That was then reduced to 20 kilometres from Sarajevo. And then Bosnian Serbs concerns that they would be left defenceless if the Bosnian government forces were to break the cease-fire and then go on the offensive were then met by the establishment of between nine and ten, I don't exactly recall, weapon collection points which would be controlled by UNPROFOR. But the understanding was that if required, the Serbs could have access to their weapons to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did a situation ever arise, to your knowledge, where the Serbs sought to exercise their right of self-defence by retaking weapons from weapon collection points?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: Not in my time when I was there. These weapon collection points had been surrounded by Bosnian Serb forces during the crisis in Gorazde. I don't recall if any of those weapons were actually removed from those sites, but in my time there they didn't breach the accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to show you a second document, P629. And again, I have a hard copy in addition to the one that will be shown on the screen. With the assistance of the usher, we can get that to you. And this is dated 12 September 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. This is a different number. It's a different document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll skip that and I'll deal with that and we'll deal with that tomorrow, and I'll go to another line of questioning since apparently we have the wrong document number again. In relation to Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think the hard copy can be given back to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, I'd just like to take a note of the number so that we can prepare for this as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to the incoming artillery and mortar fire in Sarajevo, how would you best describe it according to available military terminology and tactic for such fire?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: In the short time that we were there, it was quite sporadic. There is normally three types of artillery fire, which is destructive, neutralising, or suppressive. And so even suppressive fire which is designed to disrupt an enemy in a relatively short period of time is used and as part of that it may continue to harass or be described as harassing fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us from a military perspective a little bit more about this concept of harassing firing?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: It's designed to, you know, keep the opposition on edge, to deprive them of the ability to conduct operations in a stable environment. It's -- obviously creates fatigue. It creates, dare I say, fear. And ultimately you never know when you're going to get hit, because it's not a prelude to a major attack. It's something which, in those types of operations, are designed to keep the enemy occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is harassing fire a legitimate military tactic taught in the British armed forces?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: We normally refer to it as suppressive fire. It's understood as harassing fire, and certainly in US military doctrine it's physically described as harassing fire, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to -- you've identified that the -- that the Bosnian government forces were in and amongst their people in Sarajevo -- strike that. Let me put the question this way. In the instances that you described earlier of Bosnian government forces firing from civilian areas, what, if anything, did the Bosnian government forces do to -- with respect to civilians that were still in those areas from where they were mounting fire missions?

utterances.speaker: GRM097
utterances.text: As I described earlier, you know, regrettably for the population of Sarajevo, they were in amongst the soldiers. I -- you know, I do not recall specific events, dare I say. But ultimately, you know, the Bosnian government soldiers would fire from civilian areas because they were there to defend those civilian areas, and inevitably when they fired on the Bosnian Serbs, counter-battery fire would then return. At the same time, others would fire at those areas where they were targeting civilians or military depending on what their motives were. So regrettably, this is what happens when you have civilians intermingled with military in a siege-type of operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we are at the 12.00 point, so I think we need to adjourn for the day. I can also report that I will deal with the one document for which we had the wrong number and thus the continuation of my direct will be a little bit shorter than I had anticipated. It will only be, I think, dealing with just that one document, some questions arising from the same. So I wanted to give fair notice of that to the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Sir, unfortunately we've got to end the hearing for the day today. But before we release you, I just want to warn you that you may not talk to anybody about the evidence you've testified to or you still have to testify to until you are excused from further hearings. So please make sure that you don't talk to anybody about that. May we please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. We'll adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow morning, Wednesday, the 21st of October, 2015, at 9.30, same courtroom, I. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 21st day of October, 2015, at 9.30 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.02 p.m.,
